items.body: Turin has historically provided heavy music characterized by a sense of architecture, drama, and subterranean grandeur, while Ponte del Diavolo has constructed its own imposing structure using those same elements. Formed during the winter of 2020 through a jam involving members of Feralia, Inchiuvatu, Abjura, and Askesis, the group developed a concentrated fusion of doom, black metal, post-punk, and wave that they describe as “blackened post-punk.” Its force comes from an arrangement as unusual as it is imposing: two bass guitars form the low, dense foundation, while Nerium’s guitar cuts across the rhythm with sharp economy and Segale Cornuta’s drums keep the music tense, physical, and unpredictable. At the center stands vocalist Erba del Diavolo, whose wave-informed delivery gives the band’s esoteric language its commanding presence. Alongside bassists Krhura Abro and Kratom, she helps turn the group’s old-school metal roots toward colder, stranger terrain, where doom’s mass meets post-punk’s disciplined motion and black metal’s feral edge. The contrast between these elements produces music that feels ceremonial without losing momentum, vast without surrendering detail. After issuing three EPs, Ponte del Diavolo signed with Season of Mist and released their debut album, Fire Blades from the Tomb. Two years of touring followed, including appearances at major European festivals such as Roadburn and Inferno, where the band’s uncommon instrumentation and theatrical intensity found a wider audience. They now return with De Venom Natura, an album that pushes their established language into more expansive and intricate forms. The record sharpens the interplay between voice, bass, guitar, and drums while deepening the ominous atmosphere that has defined the group from the beginning. Ponte del Diavolo enter this next chapter with greater control, broader reach, and a clear sense of their singular place between metal’s ancient foundations and post-punk’s austere pulse in the European underground and far beyond. Ponte del Diavolo spoke with Post-Punk.com about the album: Ponte Del Diavolo draws from doom and black metal as well as post-punk, deathrock, and gothic rock. Which post-punk artists first made a lasting impression on each of you, and what elements of their work eventually entered the band’s music? KRATOM: The first artists that come to my mind are Bauhaus, early Christian Death, Virgin Prunes, Burning Image, and Killing Joke. The most obvious thing they brought to our music is, of course, the pulsating, driving bass lines, but also the melodies that are creepy, unsettling, and romantic at the same time. Most of the recordings by the artists I mentioned are also raw in terms of sound quality, which is something I find very appealing too. You can feel a visceral passion, in a similar fashion to old black metal recordings. Kratom, the band’s dual-bass configuration gives Ponte Del Diavolo an unusual foundation. How do the two bass parts divide their roles, and how has post-punk’s emphasis on the bass guitar shaped your approach to rhythm, melody, and atmosphere? KRATOM: Having two basses in the mix is both a big challenge and a big creative outlet. As you said, the post-punk genre is famous for having the bass as the driving force of the compositions, and this is in stark contrast with the black metal approach, where the bass is most of the time completely buried in the background or almost non-existent. It was certainly a bold move on our part to double down and mix these very different approaches with an additional bass, but I have to say we really love the end result. That being said, managing two basses in the mix is no easy task, and with each record we try to improve the chemistry between them and get a better overall blend. Erba, gothic rock frequently treats the voice as both a storytelling instrument and a physical presence. Which vocalists or performers helped shape your delivery, and how do you adapt that theatrical tradition to Ponte Del Diavolo’s own identity? Erba: That’s a tough question for me, mostly because it’s never a deliberate choice. Instead, it’s the result of a lifelong alchemy, a mix of every concert I’ve ever witnessed, the bands I’ve listened to until exhaustion, and the gothic musical aesthetic, which is simply what resonates most naturally within me. I’m certain that the towering, luciferian presence of Diamanda Galás, the elegant, punk vampire prince movements of Peter Murphy, and the melancholic sweetness of Robert Smith have all shaped me. So too have the liminality of silent cinema (Cinema Strange embody this perfectly), the esoteric and magical depth of The Mission and Fields of the Nephilim, the ethereal spirit of Dead Can Dance, the unsettling sensuality of Rozz Williams, and the ritualistic commanding presence of Siouxsie. All of these elements have filled my own personal Pandora’s box, and it is a box I gladly empty in front of everyone, every time I step onto the stage. Il Veleno della Natura, from Ponte del Diavolo’s latest album, De Venom Natura, brings the band’s melodic post-punk and gothic-rock qualities particularly close to the surface. Could you take us through how the song developed, including its basslines, guitar melody, vocals, and lyrics? What does “the poison of nature” signify within the song, and how did the video’s alchemical laboratory setting extend those ideas? KRATOM: The song particularly stands out in terms of the dual basslines accompanying the groovy verses. The main bass riff comes from Abro (the other bassist), who is a big fan of The Cure, and I think you can hear the influence in the melody. I also think the synths (played by our dear friend Lucynine) play a major role in giving the song its “electro-wave”, eerie feel. Erba: The poison of nature’ speaks of transformation of nature’s movement as a perpetual cycle of life, death, and rebirth. That poison can carry various meanings, depending entirely on the listener. I don’t really like to dissect or over-explain my lyrics because it strips away the poetry; it almost robs the audience of their right to give the song their own personal meaning. I believe art should be exactly like that: taking shape and living a different life inside whoever experiences it. Once it is fed to the public, it must have a life of its own. In any case, that poison acts differently depending on the eyes of the beholder, or how it manifests in the lives of those who endure it, whether actively or passively. It is a fermenting agent that can either become your personal creative spark or the very cause of your death. And we aren’t necessarily talking about drugs here, in this case, I might be referring to the magical power of humankind. Or perhaps not. Who knows? Lunga vita alla necrosi, another song from De Venom Natura, takes the album’s post-punk current into heavier territory more closely aligned with deathrock. What inspired the song’s central rhythm and escalating intensity? Please also discuss the meaning of its title and lyrics, and how the video’s changing procession of occult and psychedelic images reflects the music. Erba: Lunga Vita alla Necrosi is the flip side of the coin to Demone, a track from our previous album Fire Blades From The Tomb. It represents what happens to the human soul when, paralyzed by the fear of change or the desperate need to cling to a fragile illusion of security, one fails to follow their own inspiration, their true nature, their inner demon. As for the video? It’s a relentless procession of decay and putrefaction. It mirrors the state of a soul that refuses to be honest with itself. KRATOM: You’re right, this is the song on De Venom Natura that definitely has the most deathrock vibes. It’s an upbeat song, but dark and heavy as well. I channeled my punk influences for the main bassline, and when Nerium added his black metal guitar riff on top of that, it really clicked for us. Covenant, from Ponte del Diavolo’s 2024 debut album, Fire Blades from the Tomb, moves at a slower, more ominous pace, allowing tension to accumulate gradually. How did you construct that sense of weight and expectation? What kind of covenant is invoked in the lyrics, and why did you choose Turin’s ancient, monastery-like monuments and a cemetery as settings for the video? Erba: We didn’t want any religious undertones. In fact, I think I can speak for the whole band when I say that religions disgust us, every single one of them. What we actually wanted was to use the ancient monuments of the city we grew up in. To us, they don’t feel religious; they feel imposing, ancient, weathered by time, filthy, and deathly. And because of that, they are incredibly beautiful, just like the cemetery where the entire second half of the video was filmed. As for Covenant, it represents a gathering of natural elements. While I was writing the lyrics, I fantasized about them organizing themselves to break free and sweep humanity away completely. Your cover of Bauhaus’s In the Flat Field appears on De Venom Natura. Why did you choose this particular song, and what does it mean to you personally? Your interpretation feels icier and more theatrical than the original. How did you decide which recognizable features to preserve and which elements to reshape in Ponte del Diavolo’s image? Erba: Choosing In the Flat Field came from pure love for Bauhaus; I’ve always dreamed of singing one of their tracks, though I’m deeply aware of the sheer greatness of the artists I’m covering. The song’s core resonates with me on a deeply personal level. I suffer terribly from boredom, and I completely reject the suffocating routine of everyday life; that sense of existential frustration is practically a reflection of my own personality. When it came to the music, we didn’t overthink it. The truth is, when we play together, that heavy theatrical sound is just what comes out of us completely naturally. It’s still Bauhaus, but dragged through our own darkness. Looking across these four recordings—Covenant from Fire Blades from the Tomb, followed by Il Veleno della Natura, Lunga vita alla necrosi, and your cover of In the Flat Field from De Venom Natura—how has Ponte del Diavolo’s relationship with post-punk changed between the two albums? Has that influence become more pronounced, or have you found new ways of integrating it with the band’s heavier foundations? KRATOM: I would say both. The influences were always there, but throughout these years of live shows and records we have grown as musicians and as a band, and we have become more aware and conscious of our sound, which we have decided to label “blackened post-punk”. It’s a term that could really mean everything and nothing, but I feel it’s the most correct way to define our music. We have definitely learned how to integrate different elements better, and as a band we find it very appealing to push our sonic boundaries. We would love to expand them further in the future. Ponte del Diavolo’s latest album De Venom Natura is out now. Listen below, and order it here. items.body: I try to find the time To take this off my mind Darkwave and post-punk built an international culture in the 1980s, when records made in modest studios traveled through independent shops, late-night radio, and crowded clubs, carrying the music far beyond the cities where it began. Four decades later, that momentum has returned: a new generation is filling theaters, crossing borders, and drawing the record industry’s attention once more. There is romance in seeing music, sustained by artists, promoters, DJs, and listeners, grow to such a scale through years of independent work. The signing of French Police—the Chicago trio whose bilingual songs turn romantic fixation into a disciplined form of dance music—to Interscope Records offers one of the clearest signs yet that the scene has recovered the power it held in the 1980s. The announcement comes with Reptile/Japan, a double-single release and the band’s first offering for the label. For French Police, the agreement crowns an ascent built through independent releases, persistent touring, and an audience whose devotion has carried the group from Chicago’s South Side to packed rooms across North America, Europe, and Mexico. Founded in 2018 by Mexican-American singer, lyricist, and guitarist Brian Flores, French Police includes lead guitarist Manny Herrera and bassist Rolando Donjuan. Their style, initially informed by Flores’ love of Interpol, echoes the somber romanticism of scene contemporaries such as Molchat Doma and Lebanon Hanover, while also linking to the lineage of classic post-punk bands like The Chameleons and KINO. Opening with the ominous barking of dogs, Reptile quickly establishes itself as one of French Police’s best songs yet. Its arrangement is unusually dynamic, anchored by driving bass and taut rhythm while the guitars climb, withdraw, and return in sharper configurations. Flores delivers one of his strongest vocal performances, letting phrases resonate and holding notes longer than usual; the effect is stylish and assured, with a sound similar to a youthful Damon Albarn. That balance of spacious guitar interplay, vocal reach, and carefully controlled escalation recalls The Chameleons on Script of the Bridge, with each interlocking part enlarging the song while preserving its momentum. Beneath that movement, Reptile is built on serpentine recurrence: a sensation enters the mind, an effort is made to dislodge it, and companionship is summoned as relief, only for each gesture to circle back before calm can settle. The repetition gives the song the shape of a thought pacing its enclosure. Flores’s speaker sounds exhausted and dependent, caught between the desire to escape the thoughts crowding his mind and the belief that another person offers the only viable way out. Affection becomes comfort, necessity, and possible trap. The accompanying video, a Someoddpilot Studios production directed by Chris Eichenseer, places the band inside a visual field of overlays, doubled images, and unstable perspective. Performance footage is repeatedly multiplied and obscured, turning the musicians into figures seen through layers of damaged perception. The psychedelic effects operate through disorientation, with each superimposition pushing the performance further from stable reality. Faces slide across one another, space loses certainty, and the image seems unable to hold a single version of the present for very long. Watch the video for Reptile below: Japan redefines the language of intimacy, emphasizing care, travel, consistency, and romantic privilege. Its lyrics subtly express a condition: affection endures only if the other person behaves, belongs, and stays accessible. The promise’s tenderness is intertwined with a command. Japan treats another person as territory, where the line between need and ownership creates a core tension for the individual. French Police have long understood how desire can carry menace without losing its elegance. In Japan, this instinct becomes especially keen, as expressions of care blend seamlessly into contractual language, with restrictive clauses masked as compliments. Possession is shown as generosity, obedience as romance, and dependence as evidence of devotion. Ultimately, the promises of always and anywhere seem less open and more confined. A second Someoddpilot Studios visual directed by Eichenseer accompanies the release of Japan. Watch below: Together, the songs provide an astute major-label introduction by presenting French Police at their most recognizable while broadening the psychological frame around the music. Both remain concise and immediate, yet each examines a different corruption of closeness: the first locates salvation in another person, while the second uses affection as leverage. The Interscope signing will place the trio before a much larger audience, although French Police reach that threshold with an identity already formed through years of records, touring, and a particularly strong bond with listeners in Mexico. That history gives the signing its weight: the label is entering a story already well underway, attached to a band with a defined language and an audience that understands it. Within darkwave, where cultural authority has usually moved upward from clubs and independent networks, the deal feels like a signal that the genre’s present generation can no longer be treated as a small annex of alternative music. “REPTILE / JAPAN” makes the case with economy. One song turns thought into confinement; the other turns love into jurisdiction. Together, they offer a dark, elegant, and intriguing beginning to French Police’s life on a major label. Listen to Reptile / Japan here. items.body: Did I let you go? Or did you let me escape? I can’t remember It all gets further away The Martyr comes crawling out of Los Angeles with Under The Belljar, a song that sounds as though somebody found a stack of bruised ’80s cassettes beneath a freeway and decided the only sensible response was to plug in, turn everything up, and make the concrete tremble. The guitars combine the tar-black force of Killing Joke with the sweeping melodic architecture of The Chameleons, while the bass descends into the dense, brooding depths of The Cure’s Disintegration era. Above it all, the vocals carry the grave authority and dramatic phrasing of Echo & the Bunnymen’s Ian McCulloch. This is music with grease beneath its fingernails, loud enough to rattle the fixtures yet alert to every emotional fracture hiding inside the singer’s recollection of affection, escape, and irreversible distance from home. Despair carries a beat in this track: emotional confinement coexists with a riff built for raised fists and blown-out speakers. Atmospheric synthesizers widen the frame without softening the impact, and the guitar work keeps finding small hooks inside the heaviness. There is plenty of gothic rock in the architecture, though the performance retains the scuffed immediacy of a rehearsal room where everyone has arrived carrying separate grievances. The riff is almost cheerful, which makes the emotional wreckage underneath it hit harder. Under The Belljar moves with the cruel momentum of someone trying to outrun a persistent memory. The lyrics circle around lost intimacy, missed chances, and the maddening uncertainty of whether the speaker abandoned someone or survived them. Every recollection recedes as soon as it appears, turning love into a vanishing point glimpsed through dirty glass. Regret keeps tightening its grip, yet the song never sinks into self-pity; it keeps moving, shoulders hunched, teeth clenched, dragging its doubt behind it like a busted amplifier. Directed by Shutter Visual, the video plants the band around a highway overpass, surrounded by anonymous concrete, passing traffic, and the peculiar emptiness that gathers beneath roads built to send everybody elsewhere. Its strange, dream-blurred imagery recalls mid-nineties alternative television, when bands could look displaced, exhausted, and vaguely dangerous without appearing to have spent three days discussing brand identity. The setting suits the song beautifully: everything is in motion above them, while they remain caught underneath, playing inside the emotional pressure chamber named by the title. Watch below: Under The Belljar finds The Martyr balancing brute force with wounded reflection, producing a track that feels familiar without settling for museum-piece revivalism. The past keeps retreating, the guitars keep grinding, and the band keeps chasing the point where memory finally breaks open. Listen to Under The Belljar below and order the single here. items.body: Top PicksSinner – Boom Bang Goodbye (melodic metal/rock) It's slim pickings this week, so I'm going to use this space to highlight the somewhat unsung heavy metal heroes in Sinner. While I mostly know them from their awful/appropriative voodoo glow-skull covers of recent years, it turns out the band date back to the early '80s, with albums like the Top Gun (1986) predating speed metal semi-classic Danger Zone (1984). Nowadays, the band—named for Primal Fear bassist Mat "Sinner" Lasch—are more of a studio session supergroup, having somewhat moved away from their heavy metal roots in favour of a more modern melodic rock sound. As its title suggests, Boom Bang Goodbye is intended as the band's final outing, with the now 61-year-old Lasch similarly settling into slower pastures.As swansongs go, it's a suitably impressive one, especially compared to samplings of their recent albums. It's greatest strength, however, highlights something I'm going to call the "Ronnie Romero problem". Like all modern Sinner albums, Boom Bang Goodbye features a roster of rotating guest vocalists, including Lasch's Primal Fear patriot and melodic metal maestro Magnus Karlsson, Eclipse's Erik Mårtensson, Saga's Michael Sadler, Soilwork's Bjorn Strid* doing his Night Flight orchestra thing and frequent Udo Dirkschneider collaborator Mathias Dieth, among other usual suspects, the least surprising and most valuable of which is obviously Romero.The Chilean-born Romero, who made his name as a live vocalist for recent (re)incarnations of Rainbow and the Michael Schenker Group, has come to semi-prominence within the melodic rock/metal world of late by showing up and largely blowing away the competition on a seemingly never-ending of guest-vocalist showcases and tribute records. Romero's voice, which—despite his pedigree—is much more reminiscent of Whitesnake's David Coverdale than Ronnie James Dio, is perfectly suited to this sort of music. Outside of the underwhelming (and surprisingly under-powered)** Elegant Weapons, Romero has never really had a band of his own. Maybe that's the way he likes it, but—as the three songs he fronts here go to show—he is an undeniable powerhouse who truly shines when given the right foundations to wail upon. His tracks are the clear standouts on this album, suggesting Romero would be the perfect full-time frontman, were Sinner to soldier on. For now though, we'll just have to wonder at what was and what might have been.*Has anyone ever actually called this guy "Speed"?**Other members include Judas Priest guitarist Richie Faulkner, Accept drummer Christopher Williams and Uriah Heap bassist Dave Rimmer.As Bright As The Stars – Celestial Ascension (post-black metal) Cats are nice. items.body: 2026.07.31 【Stereo×WebマガジンONTOMO連携企画】ピーター・バラカンの新・音楽日記 50 ラジオのように！ 心に沁みる音楽、今聴くべき音楽を書き綴る。Stereo×WebマガジンONTOMO連携企画として、ピーター・バラカンさんの「自分の好きな音楽をみんなにも聴かせたい！」という情熱溢れる連載をアーカイブ掲載します。 ●アーティスト名、地名を含む諸々の表記は、筆者の原稿どおりにしています。 ●本記事は『Stereo』2026年7月号に掲載されたものです。 ピーター・バラカン ブロードキャスター ロン ドン大学卒業後来日、日本の音楽系出版社やYMOのマネッジメントを経て音楽系のキャスターとなる。以後テレビやFMで活躍中。また多くの書籍の執筆や、音楽イヘ... 詳しく見る ニューヨーク移住後のジョンへの関心は薄れていたが… この号（「ステレオ」2026年7月号）が出るころには劇場での上映はもう終わっていますが、『パワー・トゥ・ザ・ピープル：ジョン＆ヨーコ・ライヴ・イン・NYC』（Power To The People）のことをどうしても書きたいのです。 ジョン・レノンとオノ・ヨーコが1972年8月30日に、ニューヨークのマディスン・スクエア・ガーデンで行なったコンサートの記録映画です。このコンサートの模様を含むCDのボックス・セットが昨年発売されたのでご存知の方も多いかと思います。 「Power To The People」デラックスボックスセット。9枚のCDと3枚のブルーレイその他の豪華版だ。 ユニバーサルミュージック￥38,500 個人的な話になりますが、ビートルズが解散した1970年にはさまざまな音楽を聴くようになっていて、彼らのことにはさほど気を配っていませんでした。ジョンの最初のソロ・アルバムの第一印象は生々しすぎて煩わしい感じでした（後に愛聴盤になりましたが）。 ポール・マカートニーの方は「メイビー・アイム・アメイズド」を除けば特に引っかかるところはなく、ジョージ・ハリスンの「オール・シングズ・マスト・パス」に至っては3枚組なので当時は聴こうともしなかったのです。もちろん後悔しますが、限られた可処分所得しかない19歳の若者の優先順位はそんなものでしょう。 かといって、ジョン・レノンが出した一連のシングル盤は全部好きでした。「コールド・ターキー」、「パワー・トゥ・ザ・ピープル」、「インスタント・カーマ」、買ってはいなかったけれど、ラジオで何回も聴いて体に原始的なロックンロールの直撃を感じるものでした。71年に出た「イマジン」は当時から好きなアルバムで、ビートルズ離れをしていたぼくもよく聴いていました。 ジョン・レノン：イマジン その後、ジョンとヨーコはイギリスからニューヨークに移住しました。インタネット時代の今と違って話題はそれほど聞こえてこなかったし、新しい音楽を次々と貪欲に吸収しようとしていたし、72年に発表された「サム・タイム・イン・ニューヨーク・シティ」というアルバムは真剣には聴いていませんでした。バックを務めるエレファンツ・メモリーというバンドは今一つよくわからず、また曲のタイトルからしてかなり政治的な内容のようで、ヨーコと連名になっているし、当時のぼくが関心をもつ対象にはならなかったのです。 社会活動への関心から子どものためのチャリティコンサートへ なぜこんなことを長々と書くかというと、「Power To The People」を観ていて印象ががらりと変わったからです。画面に映るジョン・レノンは実にカッコよく、またエネルギーとやる気に溢れています。 映画『パワー・トゥ・ザ・ピープル：ジョン＆ヨーコ・ライヴ・イン・NYC』予告 これまでにいくつかのドキュメンタリー映画で、ジョンたちがニューヨークで過ごした70年代のことが語られています。街を歩くことすらできなかったイギリスと違って、グレニッジ・ヴィレッジのアパートに住んでいるときは普通に買い物に出ても誰も邪魔しないニューヨークが大いに気に入って、ジョンは水を得た魚のように創作意欲が沸いたようです。 元々、社会のことに関心があった彼は活動家のジェリー・ルービンなどと気が合って、ヴェトナム戦争反対の運動に関わったり、自分が不当だと感じることに抗議する行動もとりましたが、そうするとニクソン政権の当局に睨まれ始めました。アメリカの投票年齢が18歳に下げられた直後で、ニクソンが再選をかける72年の大統領選挙でジョンが若者に不都合な影響を及ぼすのではないかと、過去にイギリスでマリファナ所持で逮捕されたことがあるのを理由に彼を国外退去させようと動き出したのです。 そんな中で開催されたのが、この「One To One」と名付けられたコンサートでした。ABCテレビでニュース番組の記者だったヘラルド・リベーラは、ウィローブルックという知的障害をもつ子どものための学校の劣悪な状況を取材していて、それを改善すべく資金集めのためにこのコンサートを企画しました。 50年超を経て「One To One」コンサートを観て この公演は、ビートルズ解散後にジョン・レノンが行なった唯一のちゃんとしたコンサートなのです。ビートルズのライヴ活動は1966年8月に終わっているので、それ以降のレパートリーはステージでは演奏されたことはなかったわけです。 マディスン・スクエア・ガーデンでは、途中で「1回だけ過去に戻る」と言って「カム・トゥゲザー」を歌いますが、その存在感は凄まじく、歌詞がほとんどナンセンスなのに、「カム・トゥゲザー、ストップ・ザ・ウォー」を叫ぶとき、ニクソン政権の懸念がわかるような気がするほどです。「コールド・ターキー」や「インスタント・カーマ」、また「マザー」や「イマジン」もライヴで披露するのはここだけです。 常にそばにいるヨーコはエレクトリック・ピアノを弾き、彼女が歌う曲は当時だったら正直なところ辛かったと思いますが、50年以上経った今見ると彼女が後のパンク・ロック時代の女性像を先取りしているようにも見えます。 エレファンツ・メモリーはしっかりとしたロックンロール・バンドで、特にリーダーだったサックスのスタン・ブロンスティーンの演奏は力強くてゴキゲンです。また、ドラムズでジム・ケルトナーが追加されているのが素晴らしい隠し味になっています。アンコールの「ギヴ・ピース・ア・チャンス」では、このコンサートに出演していたスティーヴィ・ワンダー、メラニー、シャ・ナ・ナのメンバーやヘラルド・リベーラも出てきて大勢で延々と盛り上がります。 急きょ発表された劇場上映は1か月限定で、その後の展開はこの原稿を書いている時点では把握していませんが、配信もあるでしょうし、願わくばDVDなどが発売されると嬉しいです。とにかく極めて貴重な記録なので、ぜひ多くの人に観てほしいです。 映画『パワー・トゥ・ザ・ピープル：ジョン＆ヨーコ・ライヴ・イン・NYC』公式サイト

items.excerpt: 展覧会カタログ、アートやデザインにまつわる近刊書籍をアートスケープ編集部が紹介します。 建築は不純につくられる──中国・習近平時代の建築とモニュメント 著者：市川紘司 発行：岩波書店 発行日：2026年05月26日 サイズ：四六判、270ページ いまや東アジアの「建築家大国」となった中国。度肝を抜く奇抜なものから洗練されたデザインまで。実に多彩な現代建築の数々には矛盾や問題を抱えながらも急成長した中国社会の特性があらゆるかたちで埋め込まれている。『世界』人気連載「中国新建築文化論」に大幅に加筆修正してお届けする「中国現代建築入門」。図版多数。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   クリエイティブのための判断力──つくる人が考えるべきこと 著者：橋本俊行 発行：講談社 発行日：2026年06月25日 サイズ：四六判、190ページ AIでつくる手段が増えた今、問われるのは「何を選び、何を見送るか」。クリエイティブの現場で20年、判断を重ねてきた著者が、正解のない時代に自分の軸を育てるための考え方をまとめた一冊。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   芸術の発見──AI時代の生きる条
items.body: 展覧会カタログ、アートやデザインにまつわる近刊書籍をアートスケープ編集部が紹介します。 建築は不純につくられる──中国・習近平時代の建築とモニュメント 著者：市川紘司 発行：岩波書店 発行日：2026年05月26日 サイズ：四六判、270ページ いまや東アジアの「建築家大国」となった中国。度肝を抜く奇抜なものから洗練されたデザインまで。実に多彩な現代建築の数々には矛盾や問題を抱えながらも急成長した中国社会の特性があらゆるかたちで埋め込まれている。『世界』人気連載「中国新建築文化論」に大幅に加筆修正してお届けする「中国現代建築入門」。図版多数。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   クリエイティブのための判断力──つくる人が考えるべきこと 著者：橋本俊行 発行：講談社 発行日：2026年06月25日 サイズ：四六判、190ページ AIでつくる手段が増えた今、問われるのは「何を選び、何を見送るか」。クリエイティブの現場で20年、判断を重ねてきた著者が、正解のない時代に自分の軸を育てるための考え方をまとめた一冊。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   芸術の発見──AI時代の生きる条件 著者：岡﨑乾二郎 発行：フィルムアート社 発行日：2026年06月26日 サイズ：A5判、216ページ いま発見される芸術、古代の問答術、よく生きることの意味。 AI終末論に対峙する「希望の書」、岡﨑乾二郎、最新の思考。 AIにつまずき、AIをつまずかせる──緊迫の応答、待望の書き下ろし。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 掌の美術論──触覚と想像力 著者：松井裕美 発行：勁草書房 発行日：2026年07月02日 サイズ：四六判、352ページ 遊びが手触りや感覚を頼りに新たなゲームや楽しさを創造し、ときに新しい認識や価値を開いていくように、触覚を軸にした鑑賞の方法を提示する。触覚に関わる美術史を整理したうえでフェミニズムや歴史・記憶と芸術作品の関係など、現代的な問題意識を織り込んだ作品解説を通し、触覚と想像力が拓く遊戯場としての美術史を紡ぎだす。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ 建築の装飾──主体性と政治性のあいだ 著者：アントワーヌ・ピコン 訳者：千代章一郎 発行：鹿島出版会 発行日：2026年07月07日 サイズ：四六判、288ページ 装飾は、つねに政治的である。装飾の黎明から、モダニズムにおける拒絶、ポストモダニズムにおける失敗、そしてデジタル技術による復活まで。時代を横断して装飾の本質を問う、古くて新しい建築史。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   慶應義塾の槇文彦──建築とアーバニズム思想 編者：池田靖史 、小林博人、 大沼徹、渡部葉子 、新倉慎右 発行：慶應義塾大学出版会 発行日：2026年07月15日 サイズ：A5判、240ページ 槇文彦は、谷口吉郎設計の慶應義塾幼稚舎で学んだ幼少期を原風景として述懐している。後年は慶應の建築を多く手がけ、母校との絆を深めた。慶應義塾に残した槇の発言や関係者への取材、研究を通して世界的建築家の私的な交流をひもとく。 学び舎として、建築家として、学塾と歩んだ世界的巨匠の足跡 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］   人工美学──生成AI・アート・ビジュアルメディア 著者：レフ・マノヴィッチ、エマニュエーレ・アリエッリ 監修：久保田晃弘 訳者：高崎拓哉 発行：BNN 発行日：2026年07月15日 サイズ：四六判、328ページ 本書は、美学、芸術哲学、芸術心理学、メディア論、デジタル文化研究、コンピュータ科学、そしてデジタルメディア実践の知見を横断しながら、生成AIが人間の感性と創作にもたらすインパクトを考察する。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］

items.album: 【京都】第30回 京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル「京都の暑い夏」

items.excerpt: 京都芸術センターと京都市中央青少年活動センターを舞台に、第30回 京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル「京都の暑い夏」が開催されます。 30回目を迎える今回は、「Already Here」をテーマに、国内外で活躍する18名の講師により、ダンスを学ぶ人々が全国、そして世界から集う学びの場が創出されます。ワークショップやリサーチプログラムに加え、関西初となるジェローム・ベル作品の上演やトークなど、広く開かれた関連企画も行なわれます。 開催プログラム A：ダンスメソッド ダンサーとしての身体に必要なものは何か？身体の構造を理解すると共に、空間、時間、エネルギー、イメージ、そして創造性へと飛翔していく諸要素を学びます。また身体をケアしながらダンサーとしてより大胆に伸びやかに、自由に動けるよう身体の知恵を学びます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 B：コンタクト＆インプロヴィゼーション 「身体と身体」の対話を具体的で物理的な法則に委ねて探究する「コンタクト・インプロヴィゼーション」。他者・空間・モノとの繋がり、対話を重視する多種多様な接触・コンタクトにまつわるクラスを設けます。自身と他者、
items.body: 京都芸術センターと京都市中央青少年活動センターを舞台に、第30回 京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル「京都の暑い夏」が開催されます。 30回目を迎える今回は、「Already Here」をテーマに、国内外で活躍する18名の講師により、ダンスを学ぶ人々が全国、そして世界から集う学びの場が創出されます。ワークショップやリサーチプログラムに加え、関西初となるジェローム・ベル作品の上演やトークなど、広く開かれた関連企画も行なわれます。 開催プログラム A：ダンスメソッド ダンサーとしての身体に必要なものは何か？身体の構造を理解すると共に、空間、時間、エネルギー、イメージ、そして創造性へと飛翔していく諸要素を学びます。また身体をケアしながらダンサーとしてより大胆に伸びやかに、自由に動けるよう身体の知恵を学びます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 B：コンタクト＆インプロヴィゼーション 「身体と身体」の対話を具体的で物理的な法則に委ねて探究する「コンタクト・インプロヴィゼーション」。他者・空間・モノとの繋がり、対話を重視する多種多様な接触・コンタクトにまつわるクラスを設けます。自身と他者、世界とのコミュニケーション能力、Response-Ability（対応能力）を探究していきます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 C：クリエイション＆リサーチ 国内外で活躍しているコレオグラファーが、固有のボキャブラリーおよび、創作のキーとなる考え／プロセスを参加者と共に探求します。参加者も自身の創造力を発揮しながら、それを掘り下げ、与えられるテーマに沿って作品創作の過程を体験します。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 D：インターディシプリナリー・プログラム “分野を横断した”という意味のインターディシプリナリー。このプログラムでは、多様な分野の専門的視点を通して、身体やダンスの捉え方を再発見・再認識するクラスです。ダンスの経験を問わず、幅広い視野を獲得し身体やダンスにアプローチしたい方にオススメです。 ■山極壽一 × 小倉笑 「山極壽一講座」座学編ワークショップ ■「山極壽一講座」実践編ワークショップ ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 E：京都芸術センター企画 ３つの「歩く」 いつ？どのように？どうして？どこを？誰と？ 「歩く」という行為、その一歩一歩が成立する背景には、どれほどの個性や表現の可能性が潜んでいるでしょうか。本企画では、それぞれの視点から「歩く」を探求する3人の実演家とともに「歩く」を実践し、再解釈することを試みます。並置される3つのアプローチを通して、「歩行」と「踊り」「表現」のあわいを辿ります。身体の感覚をひらき、新たな一歩に出会える2時間×３回のワークショップです。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 F：ビギナークラス コンテンポラリーダンスの多様性を満喫できるイントロダクション・クラス。国内外で活躍する講師による様々なスタイル、考え方、アプローチでダンスに触れることができるダンスの旅。通称、サラダボウルプログラム。五感六感総動員でトライ!。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 G：こどもと大人 子どもから大人まで、ダンスが初めての方も、大好きな方もウェルカム！このクラスでは、ダンス経験の違う参加者が、「踊る・動く・感じる・創る」ことを通して、ダンスの楽しさをのびのびと体験しながら学んでいきます。 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 開催イベント ■ジェローム・ベル「ジェローム・ベル」上映 ■ショーイング ■大広間トークセッション ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 会期：2026/08/01（土）～2026/08/09（日） 会場：京都芸術センター（京都府京都市中京区室町通蛸薬師下る山伏山町546-2） 京都市中央青少年活動センター（京都市中京区東洞院通六角下ル御射山町262・3F） 問い合わせ先：京都国際ダンスワークショップフェスティバル事務局 一般社団法人ダンスアンドエンヴァイロメント TEL：070-6500-7242 E-mail：hotsummerinkyoto★gmail.com（★の部分を@に替えて送信してください） 主催：一般社団法人ダンスアンドエンヴァイロメント、京都芸術センター（公益財団法人京都市芸術文化協会） 公式サイト：https://hotsummer2026.studio.site

items.body: Who’s up for a hike? Rise and shine, ladies and gents! We’ve got quite the day ahead of us here on the J-Music Exchange/Rate, thanks in no small part to the particular album I have the pleasure of sharing with you all this month. If you’re one of our regulars, I’m sure you’re already geared up and ready to hit the trail with us. For those of you joining us for the very first time though, first off, welcome! Before we get underway, please give the following primer a quick read: The Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums Al and I take turns deciding the theme for each month’s Exchange/Rate, and for July, the honors went back to him. His idea was for us to talk about albums that make you want to play/learn, an instrument. Not necessarily in the sense that they inspire you to start writing music yourself, but rather those moments where you hear a particular melody or performance and think, “Man, it’d be really cool to be able to play something like that.” Less about the songwriting, and more about the simple desire to pick up an instrument and give it a shot. To that end, I sent Al off to check out yubiori2 by yubiori, which you can read all about over at the Omunibasu Substack. In return, Al handed me Super Climbing Club’s self-titled debut album, Super Climbing Club, to share with you all today. So then… Let’s go hiking, shall we? ーー Formed in 2023 in Aichi Prefecture, Super Climbing Club (スーパー登山部) is a five-piece indie nature pop rock band built around a concept the concept of “mountains and music”. True to their name, the members don’t simply sing about mountaineering. They actually go out and climb mountains together, performing not only in live houses but even at mountain lodges sitting at elevations of around 3,000 meters. That same sense of adventure naturally carries over into the band’s music. Songwriter Oda Tomoyuki freely blends together folk, alternative rock, pop, jazz, and electronic influences to create songs that vividly evoke the feeling of being out in nature, while vocalist Hina’s crisp, airy singing gives everything an incredible sense of openness. ＜Ｓｕｐｅｒ Ｃｌｉｍｂｉｎｇ Ｃｌｕｂ (スーパー登山部)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):Super Climbing Club [Regular Edition] / Super Climbing Club ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・Departure０２・Breathe０３・燕/tsubame０４・頂き/itadaki０５・いつかはね/itsukahane (Album Ver.)０６・hatoba (Album Ver.)０７・意志拾い/ishihiroi０８・ITAI０９・ハイライト/highlight１０・樹海/jukai feat. TENDRE１１・火花/hibana１２・木枯らし/kogarashi１３・スーパー銭湯もある/super sentou mo aru１４・風を辿る/kaze wo tadoru Ａｌ：Even though it’s probably in my best interest to go down this path, I am not much of an active or outdoorsy person. However, the idea of hiking, mountain climbing, camping, and exploring nature in general has always had an interesting connection to music, as it can often inspire people to listen to and/or create songs that exemplify the relaxing, calming atmospheres seen in those recreational activities. One well-known example that’ll come to most people’s minds (at least, to me and other Westerners who enjoy Japanese media) are the many anime soundtracks heard in shows that revolve around such pastimes, like Sora yori mo Tooi Basho, Non Non Biyori, and of course, Yuru Camp. They’re obvious mentions, I’ll admit, but I do genuinely give these shows (and the composers behind them) a lot of credit for introducing me to music that exert an upbeat, natural characteristic to them. While I’ve sought-out songs with a similar tone throughout my time as a Japanese music fan (e.g., Ohashi Trio, Kamishiraishi Mone, Hanaregumi), I don’t think you can find an artist that’s more dedicated to expressing outdoor recreation than a pop band full of actual & frequent mountain climbers. And just like the name of their band, and full-length album from this past June, suggests, Super Climbing Club truly does embody the sensations of taking in our natural environment. Even right from the beginning, “Departure” builds up to the dawn of a brand new day, while “Breathe” perfectly exudes a ‘bright-and-early’ energy that can put you in a confident mood in the morning. And I think why SCC is able to communicate this so well is definitely because of their instrumental abilities, where they express that lovely folksy tone through the soft flutes and keyboards, as well as the acoustic guitar melodies that easily remind me why the acogui is such a perfect and versatile instrument that’s worth playing and learning. But at the same time, it’s really neat to hear a group like them also branch out and try various styles that still fit well with the album’s overall theme. Whether it’s a gorgeous piano ballad that see vocalist Hina belt out a passionate performance, how the inclusion of an electric guitar adds some bite to certain songs (“Highlight”), or even that TAMTAM-esque chill reggae vibe heard on “Super Sento Mou Aru”… their whole background is certainly intriguing on its own, but for them to also be a bunch of talented musicians and singers that embrace their interests and convey that love through the art of music just makes them an even cooler band in my eyes. ＜Ｓｏｎｇｓ ｏｆ Ｉｎｔｅｒｅｓｔ＞ ０１・Departure、０２・BreatheIn as much as we tend to, if not always, talk about an album’s opening track here on the Exchange/Rate, I feel like it’s actually been a while since we’ve had a dedicated opener like Departure. Much like its namesake, and I have to imagine intentionally so, Departure feels like it’s trying to capture those quiet moments just before setting out on a long journey. It’s the crack of dawn; you’ve finished making your final preparations while everyone else is still asleep, and you’re standing at the beginning of what lies ahead. In an album spanning fourteen tracks, Super Climbing Club itself almost feels like its own mountain to climb, but I’ll come back to that thought a little later. As someone who almost always listens to an album from front to back, I personally love inclusions like this. Not because I think an introductory track is what makes or breaks an album, but because it encourages a continuous playthrough and gives the record a greater sense of continuity. That winds up paying off almost immediately as Departure seamlessly gives way to Breathe, the first full song on the album. If Departure is the moment before the journey begins, then Breathe feels like watching the sun slowly rise once you’re already on the road. You know those moments during a road trip when everyone in the car is still asleep, only for someone to wake everybody up because the sunrise outside is just too beautiful to miss? That’s exactly the image the song paints for me. It’s also here that we get our first proper taste of Super Climbing Club’s indie nature-pop sound, brought to life by Hina’s wonderfully crisp, airy vocals. Every time she sings, I can’t help but imagine a cool mountain breeze passing by. In fact, if I had to describe the band’s overall sound, I’d probably call it “Alps-like.” Not in the yodeling sense of the word, of course (lol), but in how vast and open everything feels. Hina’s voice creates an incredible sense of space that gives the music room to breathe, reminding me a lot of what I’ve written in the past about Kamishiraishi Mone’s singing. ０３・燕/tsubameI’ve since listened to Super Climbing Club a fair bit at the time of writing this review, and without fail, I always find myself coming back to Tsubame. To the point where, yes, I do think it’s ultimately my favorite track on the album. The song continues that outdoorsy atmosphere established by the first two tracks through Super Climbing Club’s organic folk-inspired guitar work, but presents it in a noticeably more pop-oriented fashion thanks to its subtle incorporation of synths and electronic beats. Those electronic touches are actually one of the defining characteristics of the band’s sound throughout the album, so in that sense, Tsubame isn’t necessarily doing anything radically different from the rest of the record. What makes it stand out to me instead is its execution. Super Climbing Club is, by and large, a remarkably cohesive album, so it isn’t often that one song immediately jumps out from the others. Tsubame, however, manages to do exactly that through a series of memorable moments that keep unfolding from beginning to end. The opening already does a wonderful job of grabbing your attention. It actually reminds me a little of how Utada Hikaru opens One Last Kiss, with Hina briefly breaking away from the melody with a quick vocal hook that almost feels like she’s calling you to your feet, inviting you to come along for a leisurely stroll. There’s also a lovely little vocal run at around the 1:05 mark that immediately brought suis from Yorushika to mind, adding even more to the song’s pop sensibilities. Despite all of that though, Super Climbing Club never strays too far from the mountain path that defines the album. Almost immediately afterward, the band slips into a cheeky Appalachian-inspired passage complete with hoedown-like fiddle, making it feel as though you’ve wandered onto a scenic hiking trail. Then, just when you think they’ve shown all their cards, the song makes a wonderfully seamless transition around the 2:12 mark into a jazzy bossa nova groove. If I had to say, Tsubame was the track that surprised me the most. Prior to this review, I wasn’t overly familiar with Super Climbing Club beyond occasionally seeing their name pop up alongside bands I already followed, so hearing them navigate so many different musical ideas genuinely impressed me. ０７・意志拾い/ishi hiroiAbout halfway up the trail, Super Climbing Club decides to take a well-earned breather with Ishi hiroi. Not that the climb has exactly been strenuous up to this point. Quite the opposite, actually. The first half of Super Climbing Club unfolds at a wonderfully relaxed pace, with each song naturally flowing into the next. Comparatively though, Ishi hiroi feels even more unhurried, stripping back some of the production heard throughout the earlier tracks in favor of something that sounds a little more candid while still retaining the band’s ensemble approach to making music. The image that always comes to mind is that of the band stopping for a few minutes along the trail, taking in the scenery before casually picking up their instruments and playing whatever comes to them in the moment. There’s an effortless quality to the performance that makes it feel weightless and carefree. It’s also here that guitarist Ishikawa Yuu steps forward to share vocal duties with Hina, giving the song a male-female twin vocal arrangement. I thought the layering between their voices was beautifully handled, but more than that, I really enjoyed how naturally they played off one another. Neither voice ever feels like it’s competing for the spotlight; instead, they complement each other in a way that fits the band’s warm, communal sound perfectly. I also appreciated this as a midpoint in the album. Up until now, Super Climbing Club had established a fairly consistent musical identity, so hearing them introduce another vocalist this far into the record was an unexpected but very welcome surprise. If anything, I actually came away wishing they’d explored this dynamic a little more often. There’s an added musicality that comes with having two distinct vocalists to work with, and while I would’ve loved to hear more of it, there’s also something to be said for keeping it in their back pocket and only bringing it out when the moment feels right. １０・樹海/jukai feat. TENDREThe last song I wanted to highlight before moving on to my overall thoughts is Jukai, featuring singer-songwriter and producer Kawahara Taro, better known by his solo moniker TENDRE. I’ll admit, this collaboration completely caught me off guard. Based on what I’d come to know about Super Climbing Club over the course of the album and what I already knew of TENDRE’s music, I never would’ve guessed there’d be much overlap between the two. At the same time though, it also helps put into perspective where Super Climbing Club currently stands within the Japanese music scene. Being able to collaborate with an already established artist like TENDRE speaks to just how much respect they’ve garnered from their peers. Perhaps as a direct consequence of that collaboration, Jukai ends up feeling like one of the album’s biggest departures stylistically. One moment you’re leisurely walking through the woods alongside the band, and the next you’re suddenly transported into what feels like a grand symphonic jazz performance (lol). Mind you, this isn’t the first time we’ve heard Super Climbing Club flirt with jazz. Tsubame already hinted at those influences earlier in the album. It was fascinating, though, hearing them lean so much further into that side of their sound here. More than anything else, Jukai also reaffirmed something I’d been thinking since the opening stretch of the album regarding Hina’s vocals. Her lower register has such a warm, full-bodied quality to it that I honestly think, in another world, she could’ve made for an incredible jazz or R&B vocalist. Hearing her sing against this kind of orchestral accompaniment only made that thought stronger. Speaking of the arrangement itself, I don’t often find myself talking about symphonic music here on the Exchange/Rate, but I genuinely thought the accompaniment was breathtaking. From what I’ve gathered reading discussions surrounding the song online, the version included on Super Climbing Club is actually a shortened one, with live performances extending the instrumental outro quite a bit further. I haven’t had the chance to hear that version for myself yet, but if the recording here is anything to go by, I can absolutely understand why people describe it as such a magical experience. As unexpected as Jukai initially felt within the context of the album, I ultimately came away appreciating it as both a wonderful standalone piece and an exciting glimpse into another avenue Super Climbing Club could continue exploring in future releases. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｓｕｐｅｒ Ｃｌｉｍｂｉｎｇ Ｃｌｕｂ ＞ Climbing a mountain alone is arguably one of the most ambitious things a person can set out to do. It’s a physically demanding undertaking whose greatest reward often isn’t something tangible, but rather the quiet sense of accomplishment that comes from knowing you reached the summit through your own efforts. Bring other people into that journey though, climbing alongside friends who all share the same goal, and it transforms into something else entirely. It becomes a collective effort; one built on camaraderie, trust, and the shared ambition of reaching the top together. That’s ultimately what I find to be at the heart of Super Climbing Club’s identity. Throughout Super Climbing Club, I got the distinct impression that this is a band driven by a genuine desire to create together. Their chemistry shines through in the way they perform, arrange their music, and constantly build upon one another’s ideas. The album is filled with moments that speak not only to their technical ability, but also to how much they enjoy making music with each other. Ambition, in and of itself, isn’t inherently a good or bad thing. It’s simply what pushes people to pursue greater heights, and when paired with belief in yourself and the people around you, it often leads to wonderful things. Ironically enough, I think that same ambition is both Super Climbing Club‘s greatest strength and its biggest weakness. Earlier, I mentioned that the album itself almost feels like a mountain to climb. At fourteen tracks in total, even accounting for the opening instrumental Departure, it can admittedly look a little intimidating before you’ve even pressed play. Having now reached the end of that journey myself, I do think Super Climbing Club may have been just a touch too ambitious in how much they tried to fit onto a single debut album. Personally, I could’ve seen the record benefiting from a bit more restraint. If the album had, for example, concluded around Ishi hiroi, I think that entire stretch would’ve formed an incredibly cohesive listening experience, perfectly capturing the feeling of setting out on a hike from sunrise to midday. Everything that follows is still enjoyable, but it doesn’t always contribute to that same vivid sense of place the first half establishes so beautifully. At the same time though, it’s difficult for me to criticize the band too harshly for that decision because I also understand exactly where it came from. This feels like the work of a group of musicians who simply had so many ideas they were excited to share that they couldn’t bear to leave any of them behind. Even when I found myself wishing the album had been a little more concise, I never stopped admiring just how polished the musicianship remained throughout. And perhaps that’s the greatest accomplishment of Super Climbing Club. Much like climbing an actual mountain, reaching the end of the journey is rewarding in and of itself. By the time I arrived at the summit, I couldn’t help but look back at everything Super Climbing Club had accomplished across the album with a real sense of admiration. All in all, I think Super Climbing Club is a wonderful debut, and one that leaves me genuinely excited to see just how much higher Super Climbing Club can climb from here. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４.５ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ９ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ An album having “too many songs” is, in most cases, hardly a problem to me. If anything, I’m usually happy to have more music to listen to, barring the occasional release that simply rounds out its tracklist with previously released singles and calls it a day. Thankfully, Super Climbing Club never really falls into that trap. Instead, it comes across as an album made by a band eager to show just how much they have to offer. Could it have benefited from being a little more concise? I certainly think so. At the same time though, it’s also far from being an exhausting listen. Quite the opposite, actually. There’s such a refreshing quality to Super Climbing Club’s music that even across fourteen tracks, I rarely found myself wanting to stop listening. If anything, I simply came away wishing the journey had been a little more focused rather than any shorter. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on Super Climbing Club’s self-titled debut album, Super Climbing Club? Let us know down in the comments! Likewise, we’d love to hear if there are any albums that have made you want to pick up and learn an instrument. Whether it was the guitar, piano, drums, trumpet, or something else entirely, be sure to share them with us! Before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of yubiori2 over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet already. As always, it’s fun seeing how we each approached this month’s theme from completely different angles. Happy Listening!

items.body: German multi-instrumentalist Udo Schindler has been recording and releasing music relentlessly over the last few years. The reviews below offer a glimpse of just some of his production over the first half of this year. Udo Schindler and Elisabeth Harnik – Poetry of Friction (arch-musik, 2026) To his immense credit, architect of buildings (by day) and sounds (by night) Udo Schindler is tireless and itinerant. He has some of core collaborators – see Harald Kimmig and Eric Zwang Eriksson on Imprints of Experiences below – but, more often, he pushes his music forward by performing with new musicians. Presumably, this forces him and his collaborators to adapt to each other on the spot, and in the process explore unanticipated sonic territories. Poetry of Friction captures Schindler on tenor sax, clarinet, and cornet in a duo with Elisabeth Harnik on Bechstein piano (in and out) at a May 2025 performance at Musik- & Pianohaus Schwinghammer in Weilheim in Oberbayern, Germany. The affair is largely muted. Both Harnik and Schindler have been studying extended techniques and uncustomary articulations for years, and as should be of no surprise given the title, they continue to do so here, focusing on frictions, burbles, and heavy vibrations rather than anything crisp or ostensibly melodic. If one were to consider this a duel, Schindler has found his match in Harnik, who just as adeptly swings from idiomatic to non-idiomatic techniques. Some passages are blustery and beautiful. Some are hardly audible, roughly textured flutters and other understated soundscaping. Whichever way the duo veers, however, Schindler and Harnik stay linked and measured, wandering wide spaces but most often in tandem, which finds an unexpected potential in the soulful and dramatic climax and release of its final minutes. Poetry of Friction is available as a download on Bandcamp. Poetry of Friction by Udo Schindler & Elisabeth Harnik Udo Schindler and Sergio Armaroli – Transalpine Sound Bridges (Munich-Milan) (Fundacja Słuchaj, 2026) Transalpine Sound Bridges is the oddball of the group. Whereas the other releases were recorded live in studio or in front of an audience, this album came out of a canceled duo gig. As no in person collaboration had (or has yet) taken place, Sergio Armaroli responded by recording a series of vibraphone and percussion solos for Schindler (soprano sax, clarinets, flute, cornet) to improvise over. The result is a music that wafts through space. As the other releases here attest, Schindler can honk, contort, and scream with the best of them. Here, likely inspired by Armaroli’s dreamy runs on the vibraphone, Schindler also shows that he can lean into minimalist, calmer motifs. One hears his expert control, but in restraint rather than this John Butcher-like acrobatics. This album reflects on some remote Alpine mountain range rather than conquering the Großglockner’s peak. In a sense, this is impressionist more than expressionist, which is notable given the improvisations have taken place remotely. It grapples with that tension in the colorful patchworks of yielding and unyielding pastures, unsteady breezes, a panorama of beautiful flowers juxtaposed to barren crags, peace with a soft undertone or playful danger. Consider Transalpine Sound Bridges yet another side of Schindler that ranges from the bucolic and airy to the positively bluesy, coaxed in those directions by Armaroli’s knottily vining solo chasses and the vagaries of circumstance. Available as a double CD and download from bandcamp. Transalpine Sound Bridges [Munich-Milano] 2CD by Udo Schindler & Sergio Armaroli Udo Schindler and Uwe Oberg – Schädel-Magie (FMR, 2026) The title, Schädel-Magie , is German for skull magic, which sounds quite macabre. But maybe we should think of it in terms of sounds bouncing around the inner caverns of the head, in the eardrums and the auditory cortex and amygdala, rather than something more sinister. The skull in this analogy is self-evident, and the magic lay in the music produced, received, and processed. (A quick internet search tells me sound processing is an extremely complicated and weird, and in that sense quasi-magical, process, as much higher brain functioning is.) The album, Schädel-Magie, features Schindler on various clarinets and alto flute, and Uwe Oberg on piano (like Harnik, in and out) and captures the duo in studio in 2024. The track titles are untranslatable (or nonsensical?) compound nouns invented by the late German poet Thomas Kling. If the words themselves do not quite carry over into English (what the hell is a body-branch or night machine?) the collectivity of the sounds are universal and perform a universal linguo-emotive magic of their own. Schädel-Magie begins as a wild and winding romp but quickly dissipates into extended passages of piano and saxophone constructivism. From there, Schindler and Oberg shift into a series of noirish pieces that explore a range of techniques and dynamics, though always drawn to some dark, mysterious corner. Or a winding staircase at the darkest part of night, wherein nothing nefarious has to happen but various anxious potentialities nevertheless reside in its shadows. As much as anything else, Schädel-Magie distinguishes itself from the other albums reviewed here in its mood – even in its tender moments one senses something cryptic, if not also haunting – and its barbed-wire spiraling. Schädel-Magie is available via the arc-musik website: https://arch-musik.de/project/schaedel-magie/ . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.album: Sigh, Singapore — did Massive Attack’s Palestinian flag really need a police / IMDA investigation?
items.excerpt:
Before getting into the controversy, Massive Attack’s Singapore concert on 29 July was, in this writer’s opinion, far and away the best show the country has seen this year. It was transcendent, thought-provoking and deeply moving — the kind of performance that reminded you what live music can achieve when sound, visuals, politics, and emotion come together with absolute purpose.

items.body:
Before getting into the controversy, Massive Attack’s Singapore concert on 29 July was, in this writer’s opinion, far and away the best show the country has seen this year. It was transcendent, thought-provoking and deeply moving — the kind of performance that reminded you what live music can achieve when sound, visuals, politics, and emotion come together with absolute purpose.

The British trip-hop pioneers did not simply play a collection of songs. They built an overwhelming audiovisual experience that felt urgent, unsettling, and profoundly human. And yet, one of the biggest conversations to emerge from the night has not been about the concert itself. Instead, it has been about a flag.

Near the end of the performance at The Star Theatre, Massive Attack members Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall held up a Palestinian flag as the audience cheered. Del Naja then said “Free Palestine”, after which members of the crowd independently took up the chant.

In the days after the show, Singapore Police confirmed that reports had been lodged and investigations were ongoing. The Infocomm Media Development Authority also said it was investigating a possible breach of the concert’s licence conditions.

Concert promoter Lushington Entertainments said it was aware of the reports and would “fully cooperate with the relevant authorities as required”.

The band also told the audience that it had removed a song from its setlist because of “local laws”, although it did not elaborate further. At the time of writing, the authorities have not confirmed which song was omitted or why.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Adele Chan 🇸🇬 (@adele__chan)

For readers unfamiliar with the controversy, Singapore does not allow the public display of foreign national emblems without a permit or exemption. Those convicted of doing so may face a fine of up to S$500, imprisonment of up to six months, or both.

That explains why the authorities have the power to investigate the incident. It does not make the situation any less ridiculous. There was no reported violence. No threat to the audience. No indication that the concert became unsafe. Two musicians held up a flag, members of the crowd cheered, and the show came to an end.

Yet somewhere between the stage lights going down and everyone heading home, the moment became a police and regulatory matter. Massive Attack raised a Palestinian flag. Singapore raised an investigation. Only here could an expression of solidarity generate this much paperwork.

To be clear, visiting artists are not exempt from local laws. Musicians, promoters, and venues are expected to comply with the conditions attached to their performances, whether or not they personally agree with them. But legality and proportionality are not the same thing. A regulation may provide grounds for an investigation without making that investigation sensible, necessary, or remotely proportionate to what actually happened. Context should matter.

Massive Attack were not encouraging violence. They were not promoting an armed organisation. They were not placing the audience in danger or transforming the venue into an unsafe environment. They displayed a flag associated with the Palestinian people and voiced their support for Palestinian freedom. A Palestinian flag is not the flag of Hamas. Support for Palestinian civilians, dignity, freedom, or statehood should not automatically be treated as a threat to public order.

Yet the official response risks blurring that distinction. It turns a brief gesture of solidarity into something suspicious enough to warrant police reports, licensing scrutiny, and the possibility of criminal penalties. And for what?

The audience saw the flag. Some concertgoers cheered. Others may have disagreed. The country did not descend into chaos. The performance ended. Singapore remained standing. The political nature of the gesture should not have surprised anyone either.

Massive Attack have spent decades incorporating questions of war, state power, surveillance, inequality, and human rights into their work. Their politics are not an inconvenient addition to their music. They are woven into the group’s identity and creative output.

In 2025, the band also helped establish a collective supporting musicians who had spoken out about Israel’s military actions in Gaza, alleging that artists faced intimidation and pressure within the music industry for doing so. Political expression is not an unexpected interruption at a Massive Attack concert. It is part of the concert.

Fans do not attend their shows expecting the uncomfortable parts of the world to be neatly edited out. They go knowing the group has something to say and that the performance may ask more of them than passive enjoyment. That does not mean every audience member must agree with the band. It means artists should be able to articulate a position without every uncomfortable gesture being escalated into a potential public-order issue.

Singaporeans often joke that complaining is a national pastime. Something happens. Someone takes offence. A report gets filed. Suddenly, a moment that might otherwise have passed becomes an official matter requiring statements, investigations, and administrative attention.

That instinct can be useful when genuine harm has occurred. But not every source of discomfort is dangerous. Not every disagreement demands intervention. And not everything that happens on a concert stage needs to become a police report. The urge to complain about anything remotely contentious can produce a society that is orderly but increasingly unable to distinguish between actual harm and simple unease. A flag may make some people uncomfortable. Discomfort is not disorder.

There is also a wider concern for Singapore’s live music scene. The country has worked hard to establish itself as a major touring destination in Asia. International artists, promoters, and fans increasingly view Singapore as a reliable stop for arena concerts, theatre performances, and large-scale cultural events.

But a thriving concert ecosystem cannot be built solely on efficient venues, clean facilities, and orderly crowds. It also requires space for artists to be artists. Music has never existed outside politics. From protest songs and benefit concerts to stage speeches and visual statements, musicians have always used live performance to respond to the world around them.

Audiences are capable of encountering those ideas. They can applaud, disagree, remain silent, walk away, or argue about them after the lights come on. That exchange is part of what gives live music its meaning. It is not disorder. It is culture.

That was especially evident during Massive Attack’s performance. The show was moving precisely because it refused to separate art from the world that produced it. Its visuals, music, and messages worked together to confront the audience with questions of violence, power, and human suffering. Removing that political dimension would not have made the concert more neutral. It would have made it less honest.

The authorities will determine whether Massive Attack breached the conditions attached to their performance licence. But the public is equally entitled to ask whether an alleged breach deserved this degree of scrutiny in the first place. A Palestinian flag appeared at a concert. It did not place the audience in danger. It did not threaten Singapore’s stability. It did not require a national demonstration of bureaucratic efficiency.

Perhaps, instead of rushing to complain, report, and investigate, we could acknowledge the moment for what it was: a political gesture by an openly political band during one of the most remarkable concerts Singapore has hosted this year. Massive Attack raised a flag. The crowd responded. The music continued. Perhaps we should have simply allowed the moment to speak for itself.

items.album: PREP announce Asia tour stops in Singapore, Manila, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur & more this October
items.excerpt:
PREP are heading back to Asia! The London indie-pop quartet have announced a new run of headline shows across the region in support of their latest EP, One Day In The Sun, bringing their signature blend of sophisticated pop, smooth grooves, and nostalgic melodies to fans across seven cities.

Kicking off on 2 October, the tour will see the band perform in Taipei, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, Manila, and Bangkok, while also making a special appearance at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix.
items.body:
PREP are heading back to Asia! The London indie-pop quartet have announced a new run of headline shows across the region in support of their latest EP, One Day In The Sun, bringing their signature blend of sophisticated pop, smooth grooves, and nostalgic melodies to fans across seven cities.

Kicking off on 2 October, the tour will see the band perform in Taipei, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, Manila, and Bangkok, while also making a special appearance at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix. Fans can expect a setlist featuring favourites from PREP's catalogue alongside tracks from One Day In The Sun, including music from their recent collaboration with Taiwanese indie outfit Sunset Rollercoaster.

The upcoming run marks another milestone for the band, whose following across East and Southeast Asia has continued to grow over the past decade. PREP previously sold out multiple shows across the region during their 2024 Asia tour and have also performed at festivals including VERY Festival in Thailand, Clockenflap in Hong Kong, and Seoul Jazz Festival.

Known for their polished musicianship and laid-back live performances, PREP have amassed more than 650 million streams across digital platforms. Southeast Asia remains one of the band's strongest markets, with Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Taiwan among their biggest global audiences. Their cover of Harry Styles' 'As It Was' has also become a viral hit online, racking up billions of views across social media.

PREP Asia Tour 2026 dates

2 October — Taipei, Legacy

5 October — Shanghai, Star@Culture

9 October — Hong Kong, Portal

11 October — Singapore, Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix

13 October — Kuala Lumpur, ATP Live House

15 October — Manila, The Filinvest Tent

17 October — Bangkok, Cloud 11

Tickets for all shows are on sale now.

BE:FIRST have released their latest single, 'BRUCE WAYNE', featuring rapper Flo Milli and producer ATL Jacob.

Out now on all major streaming platforms, the track sees the Japanese boy group join forces with an all-star creative team that includes Starrah, Taylor Ross, ATL Jacob, and SKY-HI, who also serves as BE:FIRST's executive producer and BMSG CEO. Blending the group's gritty, high-energy sound with Flo Milli's confident verses over ATL Jacob's hypnotic production, 'BRUCE WAYNE' marks the latest step in BE:FIRST's global ambitions.

The release arrives alongside an official music video, offering fans their first glimpse into the group's new chapter.

Speaking about the collaboration, ATL Jacob shared: "As a producer, I love being put in environments that are unfamiliar. It forces you to listen differently, create differently, and ultimately make something that feels fresh and genuine."

'BRUCE WAYNE' also serves as a preview of BE:FIRST's upcoming international EP, WATCH ME, which is set for release on 18 September. The project will feature production from Tommy 'TBHits' Brown and ATL Jacob, alongside a guest appearance from multiplatinum rapper BIA.

CORTIS are keeping things in motion. The BIGHIT MUSIC group have released their latest digital single, ‘MOTION (feat. Juicy J)’, marking their first collaboration with Memphis hip-hop veteran Juicy J.

Inspired by ‘90s Southern hip-hop, the track pairs looping beats and a punchy hook with distinctive rap flows. CORTIS — comprising MARTIN, JAMES, JUHOON, SEONGHYEON, and KEONHO — also took part in the song’s lyrics and composition, with MARTIN and JUHOON contributing to its second verse.

The collaboration traces back to the group’s early songwriting sessions before their debut. Their shared appreciation for Juicy J’s work and the legacy of Three 6 Mafia eventually developed into an ongoing creative relationship.

For MARTIN, a longtime listener of Memphis hip-hop, working with one of his musical influences marked a significant step in his journey as an artist.

The release arrives ahead of CORTIS’ debut at Lollapalooza Chicago on 1 August, followed by their first North American tour, 2026 CORTIS TOUR IN NORTH AMERICA.

items.body:
SB19 have officially etched their names into music history. On 31 July, the five-piece became the first-ever P-pop act to perform at Lollapalooza, taking over the Allianz Stage in Chicago with a high-energy 10-song set that marked another milestone for Filipino music on the global festival circuit.

Opening with 'DAM', the group powered through fan favourites including 'GENTO', 'Lawless', 'Emoji', 'MAPA', 'Wakas', 'Visa', 'Dungka!', and 'Crimzone'. They also gave audiences an exclusive preview of 'Mga Kababayan', their rendition of the late Francis Magalona classic, which is set to appear on the soundtrack of DreamWorks Animation's upcoming film Forgotten Island.

One of the biggest moments of the set came during 'Dungka!', when Chicago Bulls mascot Benny the Bull surprised fans by joining SB19 onstage, adding a distinctly Chicago touch to the group's landmark festival debut.

Following the performance, the quintet shared their gratitude with fans, writing: "What an unforgettable experience! We hope we made an impact, and we're beyond proud to represent the Philippines at Lollapalooza. Maraming salamat."

Rather than arriving at Lollapalooza in isolation, SB19's festival debut capped off one of the biggest weeks of the group's international career to date.

Ahead of the landmark performance, the quintet took the stage at the GRAMMY Museum's Global Spin Live in Los Angeles, where they performed 'GENTO' and 'Wakas' before taking part in a Q&A session about their journey and mission to bring Filipino music to the world.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

Reflecting on the evening, the group shared, "The GRAMMY Museum gave us more than a stage. It gave us another reason to keep dreaming bigger. Last night was proof that our journey continues and that our mission to bring Filipino music to the world is far from over."

The milestones continued in Chicago, where member Josh represented the group by throwing the ceremonial first pitch before the Chicago White Sox's game against the New York Yankees. The appearance made SB19 the first Filipino group to receive the honour at a Major League Baseball game, adding yet another international first to their growing list of achievements.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

Back home, the celebrations unfolded alongside the performance as thousands of A'TIN gathered for organised livestream watch parties across the Philippines. Hundreds of fans turned up before dawn at the Department of Tourism's free public screening at Rizal Park in Manila, while additional viewing events in Pampanga, Bacolod, Davao, Pasig, Cebu, and Cagayan de Oro transformed the early morning broadcast into a nationwide celebration.

The performance was also streamed globally via Disney+ and Weverse, while demand for local fan events remained high. Puregold's exclusive "A'TIN A'TIN Lang" watch party reportedly filled all 300 slots in under 30 minutes.

The celebrations are far from over. SB19 will next head to Japan for their I WaS There Thanksgiving Fan Meet at KT Zepp Yokohama before making another major festival appearance at Summer Sonic 2026, where they'll perform at both the Osaka and Tokyo editions on 14 and 15 August.

With their Lollapalooza debut now in the books, SB19 have delivered more than a historic first—they've capped off a remarkable week that saw the group perform on the Grammy Museum stage, step onto an MLB field, and introduce P-pop to one of the world's biggest music festivals, further cementing Filipino artists' growing presence on the global stage.

items.body:
As Singapore's summer party season rolls on, MARQUEE Singapore keeps the momentum alive at Marina Bay Sands with another blockbuster lineup of global dance music heavyweights. From hardstyle and psytrance powerhouses to melodic storytellers and festival icons, August is packed with unforgettable nights that span every corner of the electronic music spectrum.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

The month kicks off on Saturday, 8 August, as Australian-born producer Dimatik brings his signature blend of hardstyle and psytrance to the decks. With more than two million monthly Spotify listeners and support from the likes of Armin van Buuren, Tiësto, David Guetta, and Hardwell, Dimatik has become one of the scene's fastest-rising names. Behind massive tracks including 'Chamunda', 'Church of Hell', and the 150-million-stream hit 'Punjabi' with Timmy Trumpet, he arrives fresh from global festival appearances at Tomorrowland, Ultra Music Festival, and Knockout Outdoor, ready to unleash a barrage of high-BPM anthems and unreleased weapons.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

On Friday, 14 August, dance music icon Axwell returns for a night of timeless anthems and festival-sized energy. A founding member of Swedish House Mafia and the creative force behind classics including 'Don't You Worry Child', 'Save the World', and 'I Found U', the four-time Grammy nominee has spent decades defining modern electronic music. From Tomorrowland and Ultra to EDC, Axwell's euphoric blend of melodic house and explosive drops continues to captivate audiences around the world, making this one of the month's most anticipated headline shows.

The celebrations continue on Saturday, 15 August, as Jai Wolf brings his cinematic soundscapes to Singapore. Widely celebrated for blending indie influences with emotionally charged electronic production, the producer has built a devoted following through releases like the RIAA Gold-certified 'Indian Summer' and his acclaimed debut album The Cure to Loneliness. With more than 500 million streams and performances across some of the world's biggest festivals, Jai Wolf's soaring melodies, organic textures, and immersive live sets promise a night unlike any other.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

Things shift into overdrive on Saturday, 22 August, as Ben Nicky returns with his trademark high-octane sound. Known for seamlessly jumping between trance, hard techno, and hardstyle, the British DJ has built a reputation as one of dance music's most energetic performers. From dominating the stages of Tomorrowland, EDC Las Vegas, Ultra, and Creamfields to earning more than 20 Beatport No. 1 records, Ben Nicky continues to push boundaries with every performance. Expect an explosive journey packed with massive drops, euphoric melodies, and relentless energy from start to finish.

Closing out the month on Friday, 28 August, progressive house pioneer Nicky Romero returns for another unforgettable night. From the enduring success of 'Toulouse' to his iconic collaboration with Avicii, 'I Could Be The One', Romero has spent more than a decade shaping the sound of modern electronic music. A favourite on the world's biggest festival stages including Tomorrowland, Ultra Music Festival, and EDC, his signature blend of soaring melodies and festival-ready drops continues to unite dancefloors around the globe. Expect hands-in-the-air moments as one of electronic music's most influential names closes August in spectacular fashion.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

As always, MARQUEE's signature resident nights will return to delight club regulars and newcomers alike.

items.body:
I7HVN Returns To Qilla Records With 'On The Hill', Leaning Into Raw & Hypnotic Techno

31 July 2026

Previously Bangalore-based and now Indore-based artist Ishan Gaur aka I7HVN just marked his return to Qilla Records with the EP 'On The Hill', coming back to the seminal Indian techno label after 2023's 'Youthful'. The 8-track release featuring 5 originals and 3 remixes by Caldera, Kabeer Arora and Spain's 矯激 [Radical] is Gaur's 3rd EP this year, following 'Priests of Decay' and the launch of his alternative moniker, ruag, with 'jester'.

While 'Priests Of Decay' featured a more abstract and cerebral take on techno, 'On The Hill' makes things more tangible as it adheres to the dark and hypnotic strains associated with the label, counting on the genre's repetitive nature to make things feel ceremonial and visceral. Unlike 'Priests Of Decay', every element asserts its own identity to draw and guide your attention, specially on more straightforward raw techno tracks like 'Vulture' or the minimal-almost-ambient 'On The Hill'.

I7HVN's experimental instinct comes through on the atonal sounds of 'Kangling' that feel almost kinesthetic in nature, while 'Luminarism' decorates its breakdown with personal voice notes and sentimental piano tinkering to include emotional drama in the otherwise low-end-led EP.

Listen to 'On The Hill' below and follow I7HVN for more information.

items.body: Geology and music often operate in symmetry; we tend to write of “sedimentary layers of sound” and “geological shifts.” In January, we reviewed Paleo Soul, a rock album by Washington geologist Barry Walker Jr. This month, we turn to Scottish musician Intertoto, who references the pioneering work of James Hutton while creating electronic pieces that imitate their corresponding landscapes. The key to both the geography and the music is change, though for obvious reasons the music shifts much swifter than its subjects. “Raw Lunar Concrete” opens the set in sedate fashion, referencing theories about materials that might allow construction on the moon. This immediate sci-fi angle tips the listener into speculative thinking: not just the history of the land, but its possible future. The album takes off with “Condor Launch,” inspired by the RM Condor Marine Base in East Argus, home to numerous squadrons since its opening in 1940. Suddenly, Siccar Point becomes a techno album, but the artist won’t remain there for long. After the appealing club vibe of “Cloud Chamber,” which shifts to the adjacent field of particle physics, the variety of timbres begins to increase, preceded by that track’s gradual recession. “Fold” features LabLab and dives into dub, as if mining the boulders and discovering previously hidden minerals. “Metallic Veins” is calmer, imitating the imperceptible shifts of metamorphosis with tiny rivers of electronic sound. In one sense, the track is the opposite of “Condor Launch;” in another, it uses the same elements, but slowed, thinned, rearranged. This and “Redox Dub” are the most intriguing cuts of the set, despite being the least immediate; to listen is to experience a sense of discovery. The closing “Foraber,” based on Hutton’s eureka moment at Siccar Point, splits the difference between ambient and electronic, lacking only the drums that would make it a club cut. The addition and subtraction of elements throughout the set is its greatest asset, highlighting the impact of slow, incremental change. (Richard Allen)
